platform_facts: THE deploy VM RUNS DOCKER, NOT PODMAN. The compose project is named app-src, so containers are app-src-<service>-1 and volumes are app-src_<name>. Use `sudo docker ...` on the VM; podman is not installed. Several deploys rediscovered this independently.

SOURCE IS EITHER GIT OR UPLOAD, NEVER BOTH. For code that is not pushed, or is private, or needs fixing first: write the files locally, call prepare_upload, run the tar+curl block it returns, then pass the source_token and NO repo. ⚠️ prepare_upload EXCLUDES .env from the tarball by design, so secrets have to reach the VM another way (pass them to the deploy call, not in the tree).

A MANAGED DATABASE IS A SECOND VM WITH ITS OWN HOURLY RATE, and delete_deployment deliberately LEAVES IT BEHIND so your data survives the app. That means a teardown that stops at delete_deployment keeps billing a database nobody can reach. Call delete_database too, and say so to the user before either.

A MANAGED POSTGRES SERVES EXACTLY ONE DATABASE. pg_hba is evaluated before role privileges, so being superuser does not help. An app that wants a second database needs a second managed server. This has broken deploys that otherwise looked healthy.

get_deployment RETURNS THE MERGED redu.md ONLY WHEN IT FITS ITS RESPONSE BUDGET. Over budget - which is normal for a mature recipe or any large app - it withholds redu_md_markdown and returns redu_md_last_deploy_block plus redu_md_deploy_log_line instead. That is NOT an error and must not be retried: apply those two edits to the file on disk and change nothing else.

⛔ THE MERGE NEVER WRITES A NEW QUIRK. Whatever redu returns, it refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and nothing else. Every gotcha YOUR run discovered has to be typed into the quirks list by hand before you commit, or it is lost - and that list is the only part of the file that makes the next deploy cheaper.
⛔ NEVER WRITE A CREDENTIAL INTO redu.md. It is committed and read by the next person and the next agent. Names of variables, yes; their values, never. Hand secrets to the user in the session instead.

plan_deploy OVER-SIZES A PULLED COMPOSE STACK. Measured 8 times out of 8: declaring needs_compose makes it quote m1.large, roughly double the real requirement, because it cannot see that the images are pulled rather than built. Show the user the plan, but size from the app's real memory figure when you have one.

THE MANAGED DATABASE PASSWORD IS ON THE VM, NOT IN THE API. list_databases returns private_ip, port, db_name and db_user and DELIBERATELY NOT the password, so an agent that looks for it there finds nothing and starts guessing. The deploy writes the whole connection set into the compose project's .env on the app VM. Call get_env_keys for the NAMES first (no SSH, values never leave the VM); only if you need an actual VALUE, SSH in (get_ssh_command) and read that one key, `sudo grep '^PGPASSWORD=' /opt/app-src/.env`. ⚠️ That file is chmod 600 root:root so it needs sudo, and the database is on the PRIVATE network - reachable from the app VM, never from a laptop.

YOU CAN READ A DEPLOY VM WITHOUT SSHING INTO IT, and four tools do it: get_containers (what is running, health, restarts, crashed ones included), get_container_logs (what the app actually printed - the tool for 'deployed fine but does not work'), get_resource_usage (memory, disk, load, OOM kills) and get_env_keys (which variables got wired, by name). ⛔ get_instance_logs is the SERIAL CONSOLE and is not your app's logs; build_log stops when the build does. Extra expose entries DO keep the dname you give them, so the two behave differently and nothing tells you. If an app bakes its own public URL into config at boot (CPAD_MAIN_DOMAIN, allowed_origins, SITE_URL), generate the full `<label>-<8 lowercase letters/digits>.redu.cloud` form yourself and pass it as the TOP-LEVEL dname, which is used verbatim. Passing it on expose[0] instead gets you an app configured for a hostname redu never created, answering 200 on a name it does not believe is its own.

U=https://acsff992b07-umami3k2.redu.cloud
NEWPW=$(openssl rand -base64 18 | tr -d '/+=' | head -c 24)
echo "login as seeded admin:"
code=$(curl -sS -o /tmp/login.json -w "%{http_code}" -X POST "$U/api/auth/login" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}')
echo "HTTP $code"; head -c 300 /tmp/login.json; echo
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' /tmp/login.json)
UID_=$(sed -n 's/.*"user":{"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' /tmp/login.json)
echo "token_len=[REDACTED:value]} user_id=$UID_"
echo "== authed API check (websites list) =="
curl -sS -o /tmp/w.json -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" "$U/api/websites" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"; head -c 200 /tmp/w.json; echo
echo "== rotate password =="
r1=$(curl -sS -o /tmp/p1 -w "%{http_code}" -X POST "$U/api/me/password" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"currentPassword\":\"umami\",\"newPassword\":\"$NEWPW\"}")
echo "/api/me/password -> $r1"
if [ "$r1" != "200" ]; then
  r2=$(curl -sS -o /tmp/p2 -w "%{http_code}" -X POST "$U/api/users/$UID_/password" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"currentPassword\":\"umami\",\"newPassword\":\"$NEWPW\"}")
  echo "/api/users/<id>/password -> $r2"
fi
echo "== confirm old password rejected / new accepted =="
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "old-pw login HTTP %{http_code}\n" -X POST "$U/api/auth/login" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}'
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "new-pw login HTTP %{http_code}\n" -X POST "$U/api/auth/login" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"username\":\"admin\",\"password\":\"[REDACTED:value]\"}"
echo "ADMIN_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value]"

  - "DO NOT BUILD FROM SOURCE. Umami publishes a prebuilt image and the Postgres build has its own tag: docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami:postgresql-latest. There is a ghcr.io/umami-software/umami mirror; the docs name the docker.umami.is one, so prefer it (docker.umami.is is a proxy in front of ghcr.io — a 401 on the registry API sends you to realm https://ghcr.io/token, and an anonymous pull token from there works)."
  - "⛔ YOU CANNOT PIN THIS BY VERSION TAG — PIN THE DIGEST, AND IT IS PROVEN TO WORK. postgresql-latest is a rolling build whose digest matches NO published version tag, so 'pin the version tag you ran' is not achievable: there isn't one. Measured TWICE, and it moved between the two: 2026-08-16 it was sha256:87312d334d009ee67ee0d2fba8fed01435547cc468e452243aef5133a9984d48 (built 2026-08-12); 2026-08-23 it was sha256:fa32d116cf20cad52cbc3fad9a63b46e7fa02299d8f967168eb453d49c476b4a (built 2026-08-20). That is a new build inside 7 days, so treat the tag as moving weekly and NEVER assume a recorded digest is still current. The newest TAGGED builds remain far older (postgresql-v2.20.2 2025-12-12, postgresql-3.0.0 2025-11-07). Re-resolve before each deploy with a HEAD on /v2/umami-software/umami/manifests/postgresql-latest and read docker-content-digest — keep the Accept header IDENTICAL between calls, because a different Accept returns a different manifest and therefore a different digest, which looks like a version change when nothing moved. CONFIRMED 2026-08-23: docker.umami.is serves manifests BY DIGEST (HEAD on the sha returns 200), an image: repo@sha256:... reference deploys cleanly, and the build log prints 'Image docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami@sha256:fa32d116... Pulled' — so the digest pin is a working reference, not just a recorded fact."
  - "⛔ THE LOGIN IS PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED. A fresh Umami seeds one account, username admin, and the first-login value for it is written in Umami's own public install docs. The URL is reachable from the moment the container is healthy, so between boot and the first password change ANYONE who knows the product can sign in. This is worse than an unclaimed first-run wizard: there is no window where the instance is unowned and inert. Change it the moment the deploy reports ready, before doing anything else, and hand the new value to the user in the session. CONFIRMED 2026-08-16: the seeded login signed in on the live instance on the first try, minutes after the deploy went ready."
  - "⛔ THE PASSWORD-CHANGE ROUTE MOVED. On current -latest builds the rotation endpoint is POST /api/me/password {currentPassword,newPassword}; the older POST /api/users/<id>/password returns 404 — and it is a Next.js HTML not-found page, NOT a JSON error, so it does not read like a routing problem at a [infra]. Hit that half-state 2026-08-16 with the instance already live on the documented default login: the sign-in step succeeded and only the rotate step failed. Try /api/me/password FIRST and fall back to the id-based path. CONFIRMED AGAIN 2026-08-23 on the 2026-08-20 build: /api/me/password answered 200 on the first attempt, so the route has been stable across two rolling builds a week apart — but keep the fallback, because the only reason it is known to move is that it already did. Cheap way to find the live route on any build: GET the candidates with the bearer token — the one that exists answers 405 (wrong method), a missing one answers 404. The login response also carries the admin user id, which is what the fallback path needs."
  - "⛔ SET APP_SECRET EXPLICITLY. It signs the session cookies. Left unset, Umami derives one from the database connection string, so the day anything about that string changes (a rotated database password, a rebuilt managed DB, a move between environments) every existing session is invalidated and every logged-in user is silently signed out. Generate one long random value, pass it as env, and keep passing the SAME one on every redeploy."
.....
